An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

A woman in her 60s presented with an itchy plaque on the mid-back. She had had a lesion at that site since childhood, which had remained asymptomatic and pea sized for most of that time. However, over the 10 years prior to presentation it had gradually increased in size and became itchy. There was also occasional oozing of serosanguineous fluid and bleeding from the lesion.

clinical_record:
A 60-year-old man with a 14-year history of polycythemia vera and hypertension was admitted with acute severe abdominal pain, nausea, and transient loss of consciousness. He reported vague abdominal discomfort intermittently over the past decade. His medications included aspirin, hydroxyurea, and intermittent losartan; he had poor adherence to phlebotomies and other therapy. On arrival, blood pressure was 110/75 mmHg; he was lethargic and confused. Physical examination showed epigastric and periumbilical tenderness, splenomegaly, and left costovertebral-angle tenderness. Laboratory studies were notable only for chronic leukocytosis consistent with his underlying disease; other values were within normal limits. 

An abdominopelvic CT scan with contrast demonstrated splenomegaly and a 40 × 23 mm hypodense lesion in the right adrenal gland (55 HU) and a 60 × 35 mm ill-defined lesion in the left adrenal gland, without evidence of vascular thrombosis. Two days later, after supportive care, an adrenal-protocol CT showed persistent massive splenomegaly (25 cm) and bilateral adrenal masses (right 40 × 29 mm, left 48 × 26 mm) that were nonenhancing with an attenuation of 50 HU.

A 59-year-old woman presented with a lump in the lower outer quadrant of her left breast. Six years earlier, she had undergone breast-conserving surgery with endocrine therapy and radiation (50 Gy in 25 fractions) to the left breast for an upper inner quadrant carcinoma. On examination, there was a 20 mm firm mass fixed to the pectoralis major muscle; the overlying skin was uninvolved and there were no palpable axillary lymph nodes.

Mammography showed a focal asymmetrical density in the retromammary space. Ultrasonography revealed a lobulated, well-defined mass measuring 17.5 × 16.4 × 10.6 mm with relatively hypoechoic, heterogeneous internal echoes. A core-needle biopsy of the lesion suggested only atrophic mammary glands. On three-month follow-up, the lesion had increased in size.

clinical_record:
A 54-year-old woman was brought to the neurosurgical emergency department by her family because of a two-month history of progressive mental confusion with marked worsening over the past two weeks, leading to complete dependence for basic activities of daily living. Her only past medical history was well-controlled hypertension. She had grown up on a farm and had regular contact with various birds, including pigeons. 

On examination, she was normotensive and in poor general condition, able only to obey simple commands. Gait could not be assessed because she was bedbound due to generalized weakness. There were no focal motor deficits, no cranial-nerve abnormalities, and no meningeal signs. Her score on the Karnofsky performance scale was 50. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, performed a few days earlier, revealed two left occipital lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema. She had no other systemic abnormalities. Preoperative laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram, were all within normal limits. 

Given the radiographic appearance and the clinical decline, the decision was made to proceed with neurosurgical resection of the occipital lesions.

A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

A 34-year-old White woman with a history of obesity presented after an unwitnessed cardiac arrest. She was found unresponsive, and bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated. She had mechanical intubation for airway protection and developed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Soon after transfer, she experienced frequent premature ventricular contractions triggering polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and resultant hemodynamic collapse.

Patient was hemodynamically stable initially after transfer. No other specific physical examination findings were documented in the case report.

Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism, latent tuberculosis, and prior cesarean section with bilateral tubal ligation. She had no family history of malignancy.
